messages.body_plain:
Hi Stavros,

I think that's a good idea.  Would you mind making a few test cases
just using summarise?

Hadley

On Tue, Sep 27, 2011 at 11:41 AM, Stavros Macrakis
<macr...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Summarize has useful behavior in various cases when a variable is not
> atomic:
> test <- data.frame(a=1:10,b=1:10 %/% 3)
> rng <- function(a) c(min=min(a),max=max(a))  # range with labels
> Multiple columns from one variable:
>> ddply(test,.(b),summarize,r=t(rng(a)))
>   b r.1 r.2
> 1 0   1   2
> 2 1   3   5
> ...
> Useful result, but it would be nice if the labels were r.min and r.max, the
> way data.frame does it:
>> data.frame(r=t(rng(1)))
>   r.min r.max
> 1     1     1
> and maybe even min and max if there is no "r=", again like data.frame:
>> data.frame(t(rng(1)))
>   min max
> 1   1   1
> If r is a vector rather than a matrix, ddply gives multiple rows in the
> result (with no labels).  This isn't documented; is it intentional?
>> ddply(test,.(b),summarize,r=rng(a))
>   b  r
> 1 0  1
> 2 0  2
> ...
> I would think it would be more useful if the rows were labelled, but maybe
> that's getting too far into DWIM territory, something like this:
>   b r.name <http://r.name>  r
> 1 0    min  1
> 2 0    max  2
> 3 1    min  3
>

Here is a reproducible example of the error I mentioned in my last post.
Unfortunately the behavior of plyr::join is quite unpredictable on my
machine, and I was able to reproduce the error only using semi-real
data (comma delimited text file, see below).
Please note that the code does not work in plyr 1.6, probably due to
the bug that has just been fixed by Hadley (see email chain).
The code works in plyr 1.6_develop, but the result is incorrect on my machine.

Instructions:
1. download foo.csv at https://gist.github.com/1282106
2. run the following code using the development version of plyr 1.6:
#=======
library(plyr)

foo <- read.csv("foo.csv")  # 1000 unique records
nrow(join(foo, foo, type="inner"))  # returns 1240 rows (incorrect result)
nrow(merge(foo, foo))  # returns 1000 rows (correct result)
#=======

So far I tested the code under cygwin using r 2.13.2.
I would be grateful is somebody else could run the code above and
confirm that the error is reproducible.

One thing I noticed is that the order of the columns affects the result:
#=======
library(plyr)

foo <- read.csv("foo.csv")  # 1000 unique records
foo <- foo[ ,c(2:11,1)]  # moving the first column to the end of the data.frame
nrow(join(foo, foo, type="inner"))  # returns 1000 rows (correct result)
nrow(merge(foo, foo))  # returns 1000 rows (correct result)
#=======

Dario

messages.body_plain:
The setup: I have a data frame where one column is in list mode, and
each entry contains a vector of varying length.
I want to expand this into a data frame with one row for each member
of the list-mode column (the other values being replicated)

For example, an example input and the desired output would be:

  input <- data.frame(site = 1:6,
                      sector = factor(c("north", "south", "east",
"west", "east", "south")),
                      observations =
I(list(c(1,2,3),c(4,3),c(),c(14,12,53,2,4),c(3),c(23))))

  desired.output <-
    data.frame(site = c(1,1,1,2,2,4,4,4,4,5,6),
               sector = factor(c(2,2,2,3,3,4,4,4,4,4,1,3),
                               labels = c("east", "north", "south", "west")),
               observations = c(1,2,3,4,3,14,12,53,2,4,3,23))

There seems like there ought to be a good (simple, fast) way to do
this, but I've been struggling. Any ideas?

Hi:

It also helps if the list components are named - if not, the resulting
data frame names are pretty ugly :) The 'solution' does make sense,
though, since a data frame is a special case of a list object.

I agree that ldply(listname, cbind) should behave as
data.frame(llply(listname)) does, though.

For the archives, here's a small example to see the problem in case
it's not obvious:

L <- vector('list', 3)
for(i in seq_along(L)) L[[i]] <- rnorm(5)

# These return matrices:
do.call(rbind, L)
do.call(cbind, L)

# Try to replicate the do.call() output in plyr:
laply(L, rbind)
laply(L, cbind)
t(laply(L, rbind))

names(L) <- c('V1', 'V2', 'V3')
ldply(L, rbind)
ldply(L, cbind)
data.frame(llply(L))

data.frame(do.call(rbind, L))
data.frame(do.call(cbind, L))

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: ddply() drops a number of subsets with large data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've come across a nasty bug, and I'm not sure of its source. Also,
unfortunately, I'm unable to share the data set where the bug is
cropping up. Hopefully my code will be clear though.

###############
## speaker.id <http://speaker.id> is the column names of a number of id variables

dput(speaker.id <http://speaker.id>)
#c("Name", "Age", "Sex", "Ethnicity", "Education", "Street", "Year",
#"File", "DOB")

## Step 1: Simply split speaker level data into a list.
data.l <- dlply(all_philly, speaker.id <http://speaker.id>, function(x)x)

## Step 2: For each level of VClass within a speaker's data,
## calculate the mean of value, return as a list.
means1.l <- llply(data.l, function(x){
              ddply(x, .(VClass), summarise, value = mean(value))
            }, .progress = "text")

## Step 3, simply recombine the means from the list into a data frame
means1.df <- ldply(means1.l, function(x)x)

## For comparison, combine the above three steps into one with ddply
means2.df <- ddply(all_philly, c(speaker.id <http://speaker.id>, "VClass"), summarise,
value = mean(value))

## Count up simply how many VClass categories there are per speaker.
a <- ddply(means1.df, .(Name), nrow)
b <-  ddply(means2.df, .(Name), nrow)

## Compare
error <- merge(a, b, by = "Name")

table(error$V1.x == error$V1.y)
#FALSE  TRUE
#    133      122

## The first 122 speakers in alphabetical order are fine
summary( (error$V1.y / error$V1.x)[1:122])
#   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
#      1          1            1           1         1         1

## Speakers 123 through 255 have only about a quarter of the
## means that they ought to
summary( (error$V1.y / error$V1.x)[123:155])
#     Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean  3rd Qu.    Max.
# 0.2500  0.2759   0.2759  0.2782  0.2857  0.2963
###################

So after the 122nd speaker, the simple ddply call starts dropping
about three quarters of the subsets.This seems like a pretty bad bug,
and I didn't realize it was happening for a while.

I should note that there is nothing, in principle, special about the
data from speakers 123 through 125 in alphabetical order. The
speaker's name in the data is not systematically correlated  with
anything related to their time of collection, or addition to the data
set.

Here's my session info.

-Joe
